d.title: The delegating generator gets the sub-generator's return value
d.caption: **`yield from sub` yields everything `sub` produces and *also* evaluates to `sub`'s return value** — so `produced = yield from counted(...)` gives `produced 3 items`, which a `for` loop cannot express. The two-way forwarding is the other half: **`send` and `throw` reach the sub-generator unchanged**, so a delegating generator is transparent to its caller rather than a wrapper around it. **Which is why it is a statement rather than sugar for a loop** — the loop version is equivalent only for plain one-way iteration.

nodes.label: AND evaluates to its return value

d.title: Seven problems, and a pipeline is the right shape for two of them
d.caption: **Transform-and-filter is the shape exactly, and aggregation is fine at the end because the final consumer collects while the stages stay lazy.** The five wrong rows share one cause: **a generator is one pass, single-threaded, with no length and no index.** The two worth remembering are the last: **parallelising across cores is impossible by construction**, and **fanning out to several consumers fails silently — the first drains it and the second gets nothing**, which looks like a logic bug rather than an exhausted iterator.

d.title: Nothing special is needed for methods — `*args` absorbs `self`
d.caption: **A function decorator works unchanged on a method, because `*args` absorbs `self` like any other positional argument.** What needs care is **ordering when another descriptor is involved: `classmethod`, `staticmethod` and `property` must be the *outermost* decorator**, because they produce descriptor objects rather than functions — and a plain decorator applied on top receives a descriptor and tries to call it. **Which fails at decoration time if you are lucky and at the first call if you are not.**

nodes.label: Wrong order: your decorator gets a descriptor
Fails at decoration if you are lucky
nodes.sub: at the first call if not

d.title: A class decorator must return a class, and forgetting the return replaces yours with None
d.caption: **`@dataclass`, `@functools.total_ordering` and `@runtime_checkable` are all class decorators — the same substitution as a function decorator, applied to a class.** The failure mode is blunt: **they must return a class, and forgetting the `return` replaces your class with `None`**, so the error is a `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable` at the first instantiation, far from the decorator. And the choice against the alternative: **`__init_subclass__` runs for every subclass automatically, where a decorator has to be applied to each one.**

nodes.label: The same substitution, on a class
Forget the return -> your class is None
A decorator must be applied to each

d.title: Eight precision upgrades, and the two middle rows are a promise rather than a type
d.caption: **`Sequence[str]` rather than `list[str]` in a parameter accepts tuples and other sequences, and documents that you will not mutate it** — and `Mapping` does the same for a dict. Then the direction reverses for returns: **be specific, and give callers everything you actually have — `-> list[str]`, not `-> Sequence[str]`.** The rule behind both: **loose on the way in, precise on the way out.** And the first row is the one that silently checks nothing: **a bare `list` is `list[Any]`.**

state: read-only, so it is a promise

d.title: `NewType` is the highest-value item here, and it costs nothing at runtime
d.caption: **Every system with several kinds of integer identifier eventually passes the wrong one — a `user_id` where an `order_id` was wanted — and `NewType` makes that a type error with zero runtime cost**, because it is the same `int` at execution time. `Literal` constrains a value to a set, `Final` says it is not reassigned, and an alias names a shape you repeat. And the warning that frames all of them: **`Any` is contagious — one `Any` disables checking downstream**, so an untyped boundary silently unchecks everything it touches.

d.title: A type variable is what makes this different from Any
d.caption: **`first(list[int])` returns `int | None`, not `Any` — the relationship between the argument and the return is preserved, which is the whole point and the thing `Any` throws away.** The 3.12 syntax puts the variable in the signature rather than declaring it separately. And the bound-against-constrained distinction matters more than it looks: **a bound accepts subclasses, constraints do not — `T: (int, Decimal)` means T is `int` *or* `Decimal` and never a union of them**, which is exactly what you want for a numeric function that must not mix them.

state: T is Number or a subclass

d.title: A plain dict at runtime, with keys the checker can verify
d.caption: **A `TypedDict` is a plain `dict` at runtime — no class, no validation, no cost — and it exists purely so the checker can verify keys and value types on data you did not construct**, which is the JSON-from-an-API case exactly. Which also states its limit: **nothing checks the data actually has those keys, so it is a claim about your code rather than about the payload.** The three-way choice: **TypedDict for a dict you receive, a dataclass for one you construct, and Pydantic when you need the validation to actually run.**

d.title: `Self` is the type that follows subclasses
d.caption: **A method annotated `-> Self` returns the subclass's type rather than the base's — which is what a fluent interface, a `from_row` classmethod, or a `copy()` method needs.** Before 3.11 this required a bound `TypeVar` on the method, declared separately and repeated at every use; **`Self` says it in one word.** The failure it prevents is specific and common: **a builder method annotated `-> Builder` makes `SubBuilder().with_x().with_y()` a type error on the second call**, because the first already narrowed the type to the base.

nodes.label: So the second chained call fails
Before 3.11: a bound TypeVar, repeated
nodes.sub: Self says it in one word

d.title: `obj is None` means it was accessed on the class, not an instance
d.caption: **That check is the whole reason `__get__` takes two arguments — returning `self` when `obj is None` is the convention, and it is what lets `Product.price` give you the descriptor to introspect while `product.price` gives you the value.** The rule next to it is absolute: **never store per-instance state on the descriptor, because one descriptor object serves every instance of the class** — so `self._value = x` makes every product share a price, and the bug looks like a caching problem. **Store it in `obj.__dict__` under the name `__set_name__` gave you.**

d.title: Data or non-data decides who wins against the instance dict
d.caption: **A data descriptor defines `__set__` and takes precedence over the instance `__dict__`; a non-data descriptor does not, so an instance attribute shadows it** — which is 4.2's lookup order with the reason attached. That is why `cached_property` works at all: **it is non-data, so once it writes the value into `obj.__dict__` the second access never reaches the descriptor.** And it is why it fails on `__slots__`: **`TypeError: No '__dict__' attribute on 'WithSlots' instance to cache 'area'`** — the mechanism it depends on was removed.

d.title: Two bases with unrelated metaclasses cannot be combined at all
d.caption: **`TypeError: metaclass conflict: the metaclass of a derived class must be a (non-strict) subclass of the metaclasses of all its bases`** — raised at class definition, and there is no way around it from the subclass. Which is the strongest practical argument against metaclasses: **inheriting from two libraries that each use one is simply impossible**, and you cannot fix it without changing one of the libraries. **`__init_subclass__` has no such problem**, which is why it exists and why it is the right tool for almost everything a metaclass was once used for.

nodes.label: And you cannot fix it from C

d.title: Six parameters, five kinds, and `bind` turns a call into a dict
d.caption: **`inspect.signature` recovers the full parameter list with each one's kind — `POSITIONAL_OR_KEYWORD`, `VAR_POSITIONAL`, `KEYWORD_ONLY`, `VAR_KEYWORD`** — which is how a framework decides what to inject without being told. The pair that does the real work is `bind` and `apply_defaults`: **a call becomes `{'source': ..., 'amount': 500, 'tags': (), 'dry_run': True, 'extra': {}}`, with defaults filled in** — and a wrong call becomes a readable error, **`missing a required argument: 'target'`**, before anything runs.

d.title: `__annotations__` gives you strings; `get_type_hints` gives you the types
d.caption: **With `from __future__ import annotations`, or on Python 3.14 by default, annotations are stored as strings — `{'user': 'User', 'limit': 'int'}` — so reading `__annotations__` directly gives you text that happens to look like a type.** `typing.get_type_hints(fn)` resolves them against the defining module's namespace and returns real objects: **`{'user': <class 'User'>, ...}`.** Which is the difference between a framework that works and one that fails on a forward reference — **and the resolution can itself raise `NameError` if the name is only available under `TYPE_CHECKING`.**

d.title: Seven functions, and two of them fail where you least expect
d.caption: **`getsource` needs the file to exist, so it fails in a zipapp, in a REPL and in anything that compiled from a string** — which is the one to guard rather than assume. **`getdoc` is better than `obj.__doc__` because it dedents *and* follows inheritance**, so an overridden method with no docstring still reports the base's. And the row frameworks are built on: **`iscoroutinefunction` is how a framework decides whether to `await`** — which is why decorating an async function with a sync wrapper breaks dispatch, unless `wraps` preserved it.

d.title: A leak rises forever; fragmentation flattens
d.caption: **The two sequences are the whole diagnostic, and they are distinguishable in five samples.** A leak adds roughly the same amount every cycle — **+56 MB, indefinitely.** Fragmentation **rises and then flattens at 201 MB**, because the allocator is holding freed arenas it cannot return to the OS rather than retaining live objects. Which matters because **only the first has a fix in your code**: the second is addressed by allocation patterns, a different allocator, or restarting the worker, **and `tracemalloc` will show you nothing growing.**

state: only the first is in your code

d.title: The top line is 241 MiB from one file, and the count is what identifies it
d.caption: **`tracemalloc`'s snapshot comparison attributes allocations to the line that made them — `app/cache.py:47: size=241 MiB, count=1250000, average=202 B`.** The count is the field that names the bug: **1.25 million objects averaging 202 bytes is a cache with no bound, not a few large buffers** — and an unbounded cache is the first of §05's six suspects. Note how fast it falls off: **241 MiB, then 38.1, then 4.2** — so a leak is almost always one line, which is what makes this cheap to act on.

d.title: Six causes, and each has a signature you can recognise before profiling
d.caption: **The second row is the one people do not expect: `lru_cache` on a method pins every instance it was called with, so memory plateaus at `maxsize` instances rather than at `maxsize` values** — a bounded cache that is unbounded in what it retains. The fourth is similarly quiet: **a `defaultdict` read with arbitrary keys creates entries for keys nobody set**, so reading is a write. And the last: **objects never collected despite going out of scope points at a closure or a descriptor keyed by instance** — `WeakKeyDictionary`.
